tips.title: Four shapes to know on sight
tips.body: **Linear** is a straight line. **Quadratic** is a U (or an upside-down U). **Cubic** is an S that runs from bottom-left to top-right. **Reciprocal** is two separate arms in opposite corners. Matching an equation to a picture is a whole question, and it takes seconds once these are known.

tips.title: The highest power decides the shape
tips.body: Look at the biggest power of $x$. $x^1$ is a line, $x^2$ a parabola, $x^3$ a cubic. $\frac{1}{x}$ is the reciprocal. Everything else in the equation only shifts, stretches or flips that basic shape.

tips.title: A minus in front flips it
tips.body: $y = -x^3$ is $y = x^3$ reflected in the $x$-axis: it runs from **top-left to bottom-right** instead. $y = -\frac{1}{x}$ puts the arms in the **other** two corners. The shape is the same; the sign chooses the direction.

tips.title: The reciprocal never touches the axes
tips.body: $y = \frac{1}{x}$ has **no value at $x = 0$** — you cannot divide by zero — and is **never zero** for any $x$. So the curve gets ever closer to both axes and never meets them. Those axes are called **asymptotes**, and a sketch that crosses one is wrong.

tips.title: Plot a table, then look before you join
tips.body: To draw a graph, make a table of values, plot the points, and **look at the shape** you expect before joining them. A cubic is one smooth S. If a point sits off that S, the arithmetic for it is wrong — check it rather than drawing a kink.

why.matters:
Straight lines and parabolas cover a lot, and two very ordinary situations are neither.

When two quantities trade off so that their **product** stays fixed — speed and journey time, people and hours, miles per gallon and gallons per mile — you get $y = \tfrac{k}{x}$: two separate arms, steep near one axis and flattening along the other. Its most useful feature is the one beginners report as a mistake. It never reaches either axis, and that is a claim about the world, not about the drawing. No car uses no fuel, and no crowd finishes a job in no time.

When something grows with a **volume**, or with three lengths multiplied together, you get a cubic, which can turn twice — so its best value can sit in the middle rather than at an end.

Recognising which shape a situation has, before any algebra, tells you what the answer is allowed to look like.

examples.title: Ten more miles per gallon, twice over
examples.body:
Two drivers each gain 10 miles per gallon. One goes from 10 mpg to 20, the other from 40 mpg to 50. Over 10,000 miles, who saves more fuel?

The same amount, surely — the same improvement. Not close. Fuel used is $\tfrac{10000}{m}$, a reciprocal, and a reciprocal is steep on the left and nearly flat on the right.

At 10 mpg that is 1000 gallons and at 20 mpg it is 500, a saving of 500 gallons. At 40 mpg it is 250 and at 50 mpg it is 200, a saving of 50. The first driver saves 10 times as much fuel from the same 10 mpg.

This is why much of the world prints fuel use as litres per 100 km rather than miles per gallon. That figure is the reciprocal, so it is proportional to what you actually buy, and equal steps along it mean equal savings.

visual.alt: A reciprocal curve of gallons used against miles per gallon, dropping steeply from ten to twenty miles per gallon and almost levelling off between forty and fifty

examples.title: The tray cut from a square of card
examples.body:
Take a 20 cm square of card, cut an equal square from each corner, fold the flaps up and tape them. How big should the corner squares be for the tray to hold the most?

Cut $x$ from each corner and the tray is $x$ deep on a base of $(20 - 2x)$ by $(20 - 2x)$, so the volume is $x(20 - 2x)^2$ — three lengths multiplied, which multiplies out to the cubic $4x^3 - 80x^2 + 400x$.

Both extremes are useless. Cut nothing and there is no depth; cut 10 and there is no base left. In between, the graph rises to a single hump whose top is at $x = 3.3$ cm, holding 593 cm³. Cutting 2 cm gives 512 cm³ and cutting 5 cm gives 500 cm³ — both worse, and on opposite sides of the answer.

Every tray, box and carton stamped out of flat sheet is this question. The cubic is what says the best answer lies somewhere in the middle, and where.

visual.alt: A cubic curve of tray volume against the size of the corner square cut out, starting at zero, rising to a peak of about five hundred and ninety three at three point three centimetres, and falling back to zero at ten

steps.title: Recognising the four families
steps.body:
**Spec point A12 asks you to recognise, sketch and interpret four kinds of graph.** Two you know already; two are new here.

| Equation looks like | Name | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y = mx + c$ | linear | a straight line |
| $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ | quadratic | a U, or an upside-down U |
| $y = ax^3 + \ldots$ | cubic | an S from bottom-left to top-right |
| $y = \frac{k}{x}$ | reciprocal | two arms in opposite corners |

**The highest power of $x$ decides which family an equation belongs to.** $y = x^3 - 3x$ has a cubic term, so it is a cubic, whatever else is in it. The remaining terms change where the curve sits and how it bends, but not its basic shape.

**A minus sign in front reflects the shape in the $x$-axis.** $y = -x^2$ is the U turned over. $y = -x^3$ is the S running the other way, from top-left to bottom-right. $y = -\frac{1}{x}$ moves the two arms into the other pair of corners.

**Why it matters.** Exam questions show four sketches and four equations and ask you to match them, or give one equation and ask for a sketch. Both are quick once the four shapes are known, and both are lost entirely if they are not.

steps.title: The cubic
steps.body:
**$y = x^3$ is the simplest cubic.** A table of values shows its two defining features: it passes through the origin, and it climbs steeply on the right and falls steeply on the left.

**Negative numbers cubed stay negative**, because three negatives multiply to a negative. That is why the curve goes down on the left, unlike a quadratic, which comes back up.

steps.title: The reciprocal
steps.body:
**$y = \frac{1}{x}$ behaves unlike anything so far.** Two things make it distinctive, and both come from division.

- **There is no value at $x = 0$**, because $1 \div 0$ is undefined. The graph has a **gap** there.
- **$y$ is never zero**, because $1$ divided by anything is not $0$. The graph never meets the $x$-axis.

So the curve comes in **two separate arms**, one for positive $x$ and one for negative, each approaching the axes without ever touching. The axes are **asymptotes**.

steps.title: Using the graphs
steps.body:
**Sketching** means drawing the shape with its key features marked, not plotting from a table. For a cubic, show the S and where it crosses the axes; for a reciprocal, show the two arms and the axes they approach. A sketch of $y = -x^3$ must run top-left to bottom-right; a sketch of $y = \frac{1}{x}$ must not touch either axis.

**Reading solutions.** A graph of $y = x^3$ solves $x^3 = 8$: find 8 on the $y$-axis, read across to the curve, and down to $x = 2$. Because a cubic climbs all the way, there is exactly **one** solution, unlike a quadratic, which can give two. Reading $x^3 = -8$ the same way gives $x = -2$.

**Matching graphs to equations.** Given four sketches and four equations, decide the **family** of each equation from its highest power, then use the **sign** to decide the direction, then any intercept to pin down which of two similar curves it is. A quadratic with $+c$ crosses the $y$-axis above the origin; one with $-c$ crosses below.

**Interpreting a shape.** The cubic $y = x^3 - 3x$ has a small peak and a small trough on either side of the origin — cubics can have two turning points, or none at all as $y = x^3$ has, but they always end up going the opposite way at each end. The reciprocal has no turning points and no intercepts at all.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Name the family of each: $y = 3x - 1$, $y = x^2 + 2$, $y = x^3$, $y = \frac{2}{x}$.
2. Complete the table of values for $y = x^3$ from $x = -2$ to $2$.
3. What is $y = \frac{1}{x}$ when $x = 4$? When $x = 0.5$?

**Part B.**

4. Draw the graph of $y = x^3$ for $-2 \le x \le 2$.
5. Draw the graph of $y = \frac{1}{x}$ for $x$ from $-4$ to $4$.
6. Sketch $y = -x^3$ and describe how it differs from $y = x^3$.

**Part C.**

7. Use a graph of $y = x^3$ to solve $x^3 = -8$.
8. Explain why $y = \frac{1}{x}$ never crosses the $x$-axis.
9. A student joins the two arms of $y = \frac{1}{x}$ through the origin. Explain what is wrong.

For question 5, plot the two sides separately and do not join them.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Family from the power, direction from the sign, position from the constant.** That three-step reading turns any of these equations into a sketch, and any sketch into its equation. Highest power 3 means an S; a negative coefficient on that $x^3$ means the S runs top-left to bottom-right; the constant term is where it crosses the $y$-axis.

**A cubic always leaves the picture in opposite directions.** Whatever happens in the middle — a peak and a trough, or a flat point at the origin — a cubic with a positive $x^3$ term goes to the bottom-left and the top-right. A sketch that ends up going the same way at both ends is a quadratic, not a cubic, and that is the commonest matching error.

**The reciprocal has no intercepts at all.** It cannot cross the $y$-axis, because $x = 0$ is undefined, and it cannot cross the $x$-axis, because $\frac{k}{x}$ is never zero. A sketch that touches either axis is wrong, and joining the two arms through the origin is wrong twice over. Draw the arms separately and label the axes as asymptotes.

**The sign of $k$ chooses the corners.** $y = \frac{1}{x}$ sits top-right and bottom-left: positive $x$ gives positive $y$. $y = -\frac{1}{x}$ sits top-left and bottom-right. Checking one point — $x = 1$ gives $y = 1$ or $y = -1$ — settles which.

**A graph of $y = x^3$ solves any equation $x^3 = k$, and it gives exactly one answer.** Read across from $k$ and down. That differs from a quadratic, where a horizontal line can cut the curve twice, and it is the graphical reason every number has exactly one cube root, negative numbers included.

**Plot, then look, then join.** When a table of values produces a point that does not fit the smooth shape you expect, the point is wrong, not the shape. Recheck the arithmetic — usually a negative cubed treated as positive — rather than drawing a kink to reach it.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Four families**: linear (a line), quadratic (a U), cubic (an S), reciprocal (two arms).
- The **highest power** of $x$ decides the family; $\frac{k}{x}$ is the reciprocal.
- A **minus sign** in front reflects the shape in the $x$-axis.
- $y = x^3$ passes through the origin, falls to the bottom-left and rises to the top-right.
- A **negative number cubed is negative**: $(-2)^3 = -8$.
- A cubic always leaves in **opposite directions** at its two ends.
- Cubics can have **two turning points or none**; $y = x^3 - 3x$ has two.
- $y = \frac{1}{x}$ is **undefined at $x = 0$** and **never zero**.
- So the reciprocal has **two separate arms** and **no intercepts**.
- The axes are **asymptotes**: the arms approach them and never touch.
- $y = \frac{1}{x}$ sits top-right and bottom-left; $y = -\frac{1}{x}$ in the other corners.
- **Sketch** means the shape with key features marked; **draw** means plot from a table.
- A graph of $y = x^3$ solves $x^3 = k$ with **exactly one** answer.
- To match sketches to equations: **family, then sign, then intercept**.
- A point off the expected smooth shape is an **arithmetic error**, not a kink.

questions.prompt: Describe the graph of $y = \frac{1}{x}$, explaining why it has the shape it does, why it is in two pieces, and why it never meets either axis.
questions.solution:
The graph of $y = \frac{1}{x}$ is made of **two separate curved arms**, one in the **top-right** quadrant and one in the **bottom-left**, and every feature of it comes from the division in its equation.

**Why those two quadrants.** Dividing 1 by a positive number gives a positive answer, so when $x$ is positive, $y$ is positive too: $x = 1$ gives $y = 1$, $x = 2$ gives $y = 0.5$, $x = 0.5$ gives $y = 2$. When $x$ is negative, $y$ is negative: $x = -1$ gives $y = -1$. The sign of $y$ always matches the sign of $x$, so the curve can only exist where both are positive or both are negative — the top-right and the bottom-left.

**Why it is in two pieces.** The graph has a **gap at $x = 0$**, because $\frac{1}{0}$ is **undefined**: there is no number that 0 multiplies to give 1. So there is no point on the graph with $x = 0$, and the two arms cannot be joined across the $y$-axis. As $x$ gets close to zero from the positive side, $y$ grows without limit — $\frac{1}{0.1} = 10$, $\frac{1}{0.01} = 100$ — so the right-hand arm shoots upwards, closer and closer to the $y$-axis, without ever touching it. The left-hand arm does the same downwards.

**Why it never meets the $x$-axis either.** To meet the $x$-axis the graph would need $y = 0$, and $\frac{1}{x}$ is **never zero**: dividing 1 by any number gives something other than 0. As $x$ becomes very large, $y$ becomes very small — $\frac{1}{1000} = 0.001$ — so the arm flattens towards the $x$-axis and gets as close as you like, but it never reaches it.

Lines that a curve approaches like this, getting ever closer without touching, are called **asymptotes**. For $y = \frac{1}{x}$ both axes are asymptotes: the $y$-axis because the function is undefined at zero, and the $x$-axis because the function is never zero. A correct sketch therefore shows two arms that bend towards both axes and stop short of each, with no part of the curve on either axis and nothing joining the arms through the origin.

questions.prompt: Explain how to draw the graph of $y = x^3$ from a table of values for $-2 \le x \le 2$, how to tell it apart from a quadratic and from $y = -x^3$, and how to use it to solve $x^3 = -8$.
questions.solution:
First the **table of values**. Cubing each integer from $-2$ to $2$:

| $x$ | −2 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x^3$ | −8 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 8 |

The negative entries need care: $(-2)^3 = -2 \times -2 \times -2 = -8$, because three negatives multiplied together give a negative. Writing 8 instead is the commonest error, and it produces a point that sits off the curve.

Plotting the five points and joining them with a **smooth curve** gives an **S shape**: the curve falls steeply towards the bottom-left, flattens out as it passes through the origin, and rises steeply towards the top-right. It has **rotational symmetry** about the origin, since $(-x)^3 = -x^3$ — every point on the left is the point on the right turned through a half-turn.

**Telling it from a quadratic.** A quadratic such as $y = x^2$ is a U: both ends go **the same way**, upwards. A cubic's two ends go in **opposite directions** — down on the left, up on the right — because for large $x$ the $x^3$ term has the sign of $x$ itself. So a sketch whose ends both go up is not a cubic, whatever it is labelled. The cubic also passes **through** the origin from one side to the other, where the parabola turns back at it.

**Telling it from $y = -x^3$.** The minus sign makes every $y$-value the negative of before, which **reflects** the whole curve in the $x$-axis. $y = -x^3$ is still an S, but it runs from **top-left to bottom-right**. Checking one point settles it: at $x = 2$, $y = x^3$ gives 8 and $y = -x^3$ gives $-8$.

**Solving $x^3 = -8$ from the graph.** The solutions of $x^3 = -8$ are the $x$-values where the curve $y = x^3$ has height $-8$. So I find $-8$ on the $y$-axis, read **across** to the curve, and **down** to the $x$-axis, landing at $x = -2$. Checking: $(-2)^3 = -8$ ✓.

There is exactly **one** solution, and the graph shows why: the cubic climbs through every $y$-value **once**, so the horizontal line $y = -8$ meets it only once. That is different from a quadratic, where a horizontal line can cut the U twice, and it is the graphical reason every number — negative ones included — has exactly one cube root.

First the **table of values**. Cubing each integer from $-2$ to $2$:

| $x$ | −2 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x^3$ | −8 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 8 |

The negative entries need care: $(-2)^3 = -2 \times -2 \times -2 = -8$, because three negatives multiplied together give a negative. Writing 8 instead is the commonest error, and it produces a point that sits off the curve.

Plotting the five points and joining them with a **smooth curve** gives an **S shape**: the curve falls steeply towards the bottom-left, flattens out as it passes through the origin, and rises steeply towards the top-right. It has **rotational symmetry** about the origin, since $(-x)^3 = -x^3$ — every point on the left is the point on the right turned through a half-turn.

**Telling it from a quadratic.** A quadratic such as $y = x^2$ is a U: both ends go **the same way**, upwards. A cubic's two ends go in **opposite directions** — down on the left, up on the right — because for large $x$ the $x^3$ term has the sign of $x$ itself. So a sketch whose ends both go up is not a cubic, whatever it is labelled. The cubic also passes **through** the origin from one side to the other, where the parabola turns back at it.

**Telling it from $y = -x^3$.** The minus sign makes every $y$-value the negative of before, which **reflects** the whole curve in the $x$-axis. $y = -x^3$ is still an S, but it runs from **top-left to bottom-right**. Checking one point settles it: at $x = 2$, $y = x^3$ gives 8 and $y = -x^3$ gives $-8$.

**Solving $x^3 = -8$ from the graph.** The solutions of $x^3 = -8$ are the $x$-values where the curve $y = x^3$ has height $-8$. So I find $-8$ on the $y$-axis, read **across** to the curve, and **down** to the $x$-axis, landing at $x = -2$. Checking: $(-2)^3 = -8$ ✓.

There is exactly **one** solution, and the graph shows why: the cubic climbs through every $y$-value **once**, so the horizontal line $y = -8$ meets it only once. That is different from a quadratic, where a horizontal line can cut the U twice, and it is the graphical reason every number — negative ones included — has exactly one cube root.

examTechnique.body:
**Family from the highest power, direction from the sign, position from the constant.** That reads any of these equations into a sketch, and any sketch back into its equation.

A cubic's ends go **opposite ways**; a reciprocal is **two arms that never touch the axes**. Cube negatives carefully — $(-2)^3 = -8$ — and if a plotted point sits off the smooth shape, the arithmetic is wrong, not the shape.
examinerErrors: Writing $(-2)^3 = 8$, and plotting a point off the curve.
Sketching a cubic with both ends going the same way.
Joining the two arms of $y = \frac{1}{x}$ through the origin.
Letting a reciprocal arm touch or cross an axis.
Ignoring a minus sign in front and drawing the shape the wrong way round.
Matching a graph by its constant term before checking its family.
Drawing a kink to reach a wrongly calculated point.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the **family from the highest power** and the **direction from the sign** without hesitation, and uses the constant only to pin down which of two similar curves it is. It cubes negatives correctly and treats a stray point as an **arithmetic error**. Its sketch of a cubic leaves in **opposite directions**, and its sketch of a reciprocal shows **two separate arms** approaching both **asymptotes** without touching. It reads $x^3 = k$ off a graph as a **single** solution and can say why, and it can explain the reciprocal's gap and its missing intercepts from the two facts about division that cause them.
